1. The five reasons for not joining CBHI (112, 98, 67, 46 and 27 households) are to go in your thesis. You want the reader to compare the reasons with one another. Would a bar diagram or a pie diagram serve better, and why?

A bar diagram. The purpose is to compare categories with each other, and the eye compares lengths on a common baseline more accurately than angles or areas (Cleveland & McGill, 1984). The number of categories is not the deciding point: five exhaustive categories (they include “other” and add to 350) could be drawn as a pie, and a pie would suit a message about the share of one whole. For “which reason is most common, and by how much?”, bars ordered from largest to smallest are clearer.

2. Why must a bar diagram’s value axis start at zero? Use the drawn-ratio formula to show what happens if it starts at 50 for two bars of 60 and 80.

A bar encodes its value by its length, so lengths are in the right ratio only if they are measured from zero. From baseline c = 50: drawn ratio = (80 − 50) ÷ (60 − 50) = 30 ÷ 10 = 3. True ratio = 80 ÷ 60 = 1.33. The truncated chart makes the second bar look three times the first, when it is only one-third larger.

3. In Figure 4.2, Q3 has 15 normal, 4 moderately wasted and 2 severely wasted children. What height does the moderate-wasting segment have in the percentage bar?

Q3 total = 15 + 4 + 2 = 21. Moderate wasting = 4 ÷ 21 × 100 = 19.0%. The segment runs from 71.4% (the top of the normal segment, 15/21) to 71.4 + 19.0 = 90.5%.

1. Name the one visual feature that tells you at once whether you are looking at a histogram or a bar diagram, and say why that feature exists.

Histogram bars adjoin, with no gaps, because the x-axis is a continuous numeric scale and one class runs straight into the next. Bar-diagram bars stand apart, because each bar is a separate category (ordered or not) with nothing in between.

2. Using the “less than” ogive points for today’s 30 weights, estimate the first quartile (the weight with 7.5 children below it).

The count 7.5 lies between the points (10, 5) and (12, 17). Interpolating: Q1 ≈ 10 + (7.5 − 5) ÷ (17 − 5) × 2 = 10 + 2.5/12 × 2 = 10.42 kg. (The Q1 of the 30 raw weights by R’s default method is 10.57 kg; the ogive estimate assumes values are spread evenly within the class.)

3. A histogram of haemoglobin uses classes 7 to <9, 9 to <11 and 11 to <15 g/dL, with 10, 30 and 40 women. What height should each bar have, and which class is the most crowded per g/dL?

The widths are unequal (2, 2 and 4 g/dL), so plot frequency density = frequency ÷ width: 10 ÷ 2 = 5, 30 ÷ 2 = 15 and 40 ÷ 4 = 10 women per g/dL. The 9 to <11 g/dL class is the most crowded (15 per g/dL), even though the 11 to <15 class holds the most women. Drawn at height 40, the last bar would wrongly look the densest.

1. A box plot’s median line sits much closer to the top of the box than the bottom. What does that tell you about the shape of the middle half of the data?

The distance from the median to Q3 is short and the distance from Q1 to the median is long, so the lower half of the middle 50% is more spread out. That is a sign of left (negative) skew within the IQR. Check the whiskers and outliers too before describing the whole distribution.

2. For CBHI members, Q1 = 3.5 km and Q3 = 9.2 km, and distances run from 0.2 to 14.7 km. Compute the Tukey fences and say whether any member household would be drawn as a separate point.

IQR = 9.2 − 3.5 = 5.7 km; 1.5 × IQR = 8.55 km. Lower fence = 3.5 − 8.55 = −5.05 km; upper fence = 9.2 + 8.55 = 17.75 km. The minimum (0.2 km) and maximum (14.7 km) both lie inside, so no household is drawn separately, and the whiskers reach the minimum and the maximum. (With the unrounded Q3 of 9.175 km the fences are −5.01 and 17.69 km; the conclusion is the same.)

3. Why might you prefer a stem-and-leaf plot to a histogram for a small dataset?

It shows the shape of the distribution and still keeps every value, so you can read back any observation and count the median and quartiles straight off it. A histogram loses the individual values once they are grouped. With a small dataset the individual values still carry information, and the plot stays short enough to read.

1. A district’s measles cases rose from 50 to 200 in five years, while a neighbouring district’s rose from 500 to 1,000. On a semi-log graph, which line is steeper? Give each district’s annual growth factor.

First district: 200 ÷ 50 = 4-fold in 5 years; annual factor = 4^(1/5) = 1.32 (32% a year). Second district: 1,000 ÷ 500 = 2-fold; annual factor = 2^(1/5) = 1.15 (15% a year). On a semi-log graph the slope is log(annual factor), so the first district’s line is steeper (log₁₀ 1.32 = 0.120 vs log₁₀ 1.15 = 0.060 per year), even though the second district added more cases (500 vs 150).

2. In a point-source outbreak the first case fell ill 30 hours after a community lunch and the last 90 hours after it. The agent’s incubation period is taken as 24 to 96 hours. Using the first- and last-case rules, where does the exposure window fall relative to the lunch?

Latest possible exposure = first onset − minimum incubation = 30 − 24 = 6 hours after the lunch. Earliest possible exposure = last onset − maximum incubation = 90 − 96 = −6, that is 6 hours before the lunch. The window runs from 6 hours before to 6 hours after the lunch, so it contains the lunch, which is consistent with the lunch being the source. Food-specific attack rates are the next step.

3. An epi curve rises steadily for three weeks and stays high. Which of the three patterns does this suggest, and what kind of source would you look for?

A continuous common-source outbreak: the curve “rises gradually and might plateau” (CDC, n.d.-a). Look for a source that keeps exposing people, such as a contaminated well or water supply, rather than a single meal (which would give a sharp rise and fall within one incubation period) or person-to-person spread (successive peaks one incubation period apart).

1. Ward P had 40 dengue cases in a population of 50,000; ward Q had 15 cases in 6,000. Which has more dots on a spot map, and which is darker on a choropleth map? Give both rates per 10,000.

Ward P has more dots (40 vs 15). Rates: P = 40 ÷ 50,000 × 10,000 = 8.0 per 10,000; Q = 15 ÷ 6,000 × 10,000 = 25.0 per 10,000. Ward Q is darker on the choropleth map: its risk is about three times ward P’s.

2. A district’s population is 34% aged 0–14, 60% aged 15–64 and 6% aged 65+. Compute its age dependency ratio. Is its pyramid more likely to be expansive or constrictive?

Dependency ratio = (34 + 6) ÷ 60 × 100 = 66.7 dependents per 100 working-age people (young-age ratio 34 ÷ 60 × 100 = 56.7; old-age ratio 6 ÷ 60 × 100 = 10.0). A third of the population is under 15 and the burden is almost all children, so the pyramid is more likely expansive (broad base).

3. A poster shows PHC coverage of 60% by a syringe 3 cm tall and 1 cm wide, and 90% by a syringe 4.5 cm tall and 1.5 cm wide. What ratio does the poster’s area suggest, and what is the true ratio?

Areas: 3 × 1 = 3 cm² and 4.5 × 1.5 = 6.75 cm². The poster suggests 6.75 ÷ 3 = 2.25 times the coverage. The true ratio is 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5. Scaling both dimensions by 1.5 multiplied the area by 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. Draw more symbols, or bars, instead.
